options.metric: Total police-reported crash count in the night period and in the day period
options.denominator: Equal 12-hour time windows over the same included dates and years (2013-2025); not a traffic-exposure denominator
options.reason: A careful analyst may first compare reported crash volume in equal-length nighttime and daytime windows.
options.answer: Across 2013-2025, there were 681,531 police-reported crashes from 7 p.m. to 6:59 a.m. versus 1,450,687 from 7 a.m. to 6:59 p.m., so reported crash volume was lower at night, though this does not establish lower travel risk.
options.interpretation: This framing answers the question only in terms of crash volume: there were 681,531 night crashes versus 1,450,687 daytime crashes across the same 13 years. It is defensible because each comparison window is 12 hours and both use the same dates, but total reports are not a rate of danger. It leaves travel-exposure risk and crash severity unanswered because the file has no traffic-volume, trip, or mileage denominator. The check retained all 2,132,218 selected-year rows with usable date/time (0 missing date/time), omitted the partial observed-bound years 2012 and 2026, and kept 23,787 midnight rows (1.12%) as night despite possible default-time ambiguity.

options.metric: Percentage of police-reported crashes with at least one person reported injured or killed
options.denominator: All included crashes in the corresponding day/night period with known, nonnegative number_of_persons_injured and number_of_persons_killed
options.reason: A careful analyst may focus on whether a reported crash is more likely to involve injury or death at night, conditional on a crash occurring.
options.answer: Among crashes with known person counts, 28.2% of night crashes involved an injury or fatality versus 23.0% of daytime crashes, a 5.2-percentage-point difference.
options.interpretation: This framing answers whether a reported crash is more likely to involve harm, not whether a trip is more likely to crash: injury/fatality involvement was 28.2% at night versus 23.0% by day (5.2 percentage points higher). It is defensible because it compares a defined reported consequence among crashes in equal 12-hour periods, conditional on a crash being reported. It leaves exposure-adjusted risk, unreported crashes, and separate fatality-only or person-level rates unanswered. Checks found 42 of 2,132,218 valid-time rows (0.002%) missing either person count; these were excluded, while zero counts (1,608,886 injured-count zeros and 2,128,911 killed-count zeros) and 23,787 midnight timestamps (1.12%) were retained, and partial 2012/2026 were omitted.
